opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of those questions where my answer has genuinely shifted over time, and I expect it to keep shifting.

Right now, the way I think about it is in terms of *marginal* harm. Most of the attacks a model can help you construct today are things a reasonably competent person could already do with some time and a search engine. So the question isn't "can the model write an exploit?" It's "does the model let someone do something they couldn't have done otherwise, or do it at a scale they couldn't have reached otherwise?" For a lot of current capabilities, I think the honest answer is: a little, but not dramatically.

That's exactly the part I expect to change. There are two ways it could go. The first is the uplift for unsophisticated attackers. If models get good enough that someone with essentially no expertise can say "go break into this thing" and it works end to end, that's a qualitatively different world. The barrier to entry for a lot of attacks has always been skill, and skill is precisely what these systems are getting better at providing.

The second, which I worry about maybe even more, is scale and cost. Plenty of attacks aren't hard so much as tedious. Finding the one vulnerable configuration among thousands of targets, or reading through a huge codebase looking for the subtle bug. Humans don't do that because it isn't worth their time. If a model can do it for a few dollars, the economics of attacking flip completely. Things that were never worth exploiting suddenly are.

The thing I try to be careful about is not just extrapolating smoothly. Capabilities in this area seem to arrive somewhat suddenly. A model can't really do a task, and then a generation later it can do it reliably. So I don't think it makes sense to say "today the harm is low, so tomorrow it'll be a bit higher." I'd rather say: here are the specific capabilities that would change my assessment, let's measure them carefully, and let's be ready before they show up rather than after.

And to be fair to the other side, the same capabilities help defenders. If a model can find bugs, you can run it on your own code first. I'm somewhat optimistic about that in the long run. My concern is mostly about the transition period, where offensive use is easy to deploy immediately and defensive adoption takes years. That gap is where I'd expect most of the real harm to happen.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is a place where I have to be honest about the fact that my view has already shifted, and I expect it to keep shifting.

A few years ago my position was pretty comfortable. Language models could write code, sure, but if you asked one to find a vulnerability in some real piece of software, it mostly just hallucinated something plausible-sounding and wrong. And the people who actually do offensive security for a living could look at that output and laugh. So the honest assessment was: the harm is low, because the capability is low. Anyone who could use these tools to attack things could already do it faster themselves.

The thing I always tried to be careful about, though, is separating two different claims. One is "the models can't do this today." The other is "the models won't be able to do this." The first was a measurement, and I was happy to make it. The second is a prediction, and I don't think anyone has a great track record on those.

And what's happened is that the measurement has changed. If I take a model now and point it at a reasonably large codebase and say, find me a memory safety bug, it will sometimes actually find one. Not every time. Often it's finding things that a fuzzer would have found. But sometimes it's finding things that required understanding what the code was supposed to do and noticing that it didn't do that. That's the kind of thing I would have told you two years ago was pretty far off.

So how does my assessment change? I think the key question becomes less about whether the model can construct an attack and more about who it gives that ability to. The people I worry about least are the sophisticated nation-state actors. They already have the capability. A model that's roughly as good as a mid-level security researcher doesn't change their calculus very much. The people I worry about more are the ones who are currently constrained by skill rather than by motivation. There's a large population of people who would happily break into things if they could, and historically the barrier has been that it's hard. If the barrier drops from "you need five years of experience" to "you need to know how to prompt a model and wait," that's a meaningful change in the threat landscape, even if the attacks themselves aren't novel.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to resist the framing where offense is the only thing that's improving. The same model that can find a bug can find it for the defender first. And historically a lot of the reason software is insecure isn't that attackers are brilliant, it's that nobody looked. If you can make looking cheap, that's genuinely good. But I don't think it's automatically balanced. Defense has to be right everywhere, and offense only has to be right once, and that asymmetry doesn't go away just because both sides have the same tool.

So if you push me, I'd say my assessment of the harm goes up as the models improve, but not linearly, and not in the way people usually imagine. I don't expect a model to one day produce some superweapon exploit that no human could have found. I expect a lot more of the mundane stuff to happen a lot more often, done by people who couldn't have done it before. And I think the right response to that is less about stopping the models from knowing things and more about finally fixing the software, because the excuse that nobody would bother to look is about to stop being true.

astra-6.text:
I think it could change quite a lot. My assessment today is largely about the marginal contribution of the model. If someone can already find an attack with a quick search, and the model gives them essentially the same thing, then it hasn’t added very much capability. But that’s not a claim that models will always be harmless in this setting.

If you get to a point where a model can discover a new vulnerability, figure out how to exploit it, and reliably carry out an attack with very little human guidance, that’s a different situation. Now you’re potentially giving someone a capability they wouldn’t otherwise have, or allowing an expert to operate at a much larger scale.

So I’d want to keep asking: what can someone accomplish with the model that they couldn’t accomplish without it? And how much cheaper or faster does it become? As models improve, those answers could become much more concerning. The fact that an attack demonstration today doesn’t establish a large increase in harm shouldn’t be taken as evidence that a future system won’t.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the assessment could change quite a lot. The question I care about is how much the model helps someone do something they otherwise couldn’t do. If it produces an attack that an expert could write in five minutes, that’s useful, but it’s a relatively small change. If it lets someone with very little expertise carry out an attack that previously required a specialist, that’s much more concerning.

And as models improve, I’d expect us to move further in that direction. Right now, a model might give you a plausible suggestion, but you still need someone who can recognize when it’s wrong, debug it, and put all the pieces together. If the model can do that entire loop itself—try something, interpret the result, revise the attack—then the human expertise required could drop substantially.

So I wouldn’t take an assessment of today’s systems as a reassuring statement about future systems. We need to keep measuring the actual increase in capability: who can succeed with the model, against what targets, and how that compares to what they could do without it.
